messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Children Present: Being around children, Media / News: Related news, Known People: Related people
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Farid Mansour is a 78-year-old Lebanese-American man who has worked as a roofer for most of his adult life, a trade he took up shortly after immigrating to the United States in his late twenties. He is married, the father of four grown children, and until recently was known among his family as a man of quiet steadiness — someone who got up before dawn, worked with his hands, and did not speak much about what troubled him. He presented for treatment following what his wife described as a year of progressive withdrawal and distress that she could no longer attribute to ordinary aging.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Farid was contracted to help reroof a commercial building that had previously housed a chemical storage facility. He and two younger crew members were well into the job when they began cutting through older roofing layers that concealed what was later identified as residual industrial solvent — a volatile, toxic compound that had been improperly sealed beneath successive layers of tar and membrane. Within minutes of the material being disturbed, Farid experienced a burning sensation in his throat and eyes, a sudden inability to draw a full breath, and what he described as a feeling that the air itself had turned against him. He recalled the smell — acrid, chemical, almost sweet — and the sight of a fine yellowish vapor rising from the cut surface in the afternoon heat. One of the younger men on the crew, a man in his thirties with children Farid had met at a company barbecue, collapsed and had to be carried from the roof. Farid made it down the ladder himself but lost consciousness briefly in the parking lot. He spent two nights in hospital and was discharged with no permanent pulmonary injury documented, though he continued to experience shortness of breath and fatigue in the weeks that followed.

In the months after the incident, Farid noticed that the memory of that afternoon did not behave as other memories did. When he tried deliberately to sit with what had happened — to reconstruct it, to make sense of it — he found the details slipping away from him, the sequence dissolving before he could hold it. And yet the memory arrived unbidden and with force: while watching television, while lying in bed, while eating dinner with his wife. What disturbed him most was that sometimes there was no image at all, only the feeling — a sudden tightening in his chest, a wave of dread so complete and sourceless that he could not explain it to himself or to anyone else. He had come to believe that something had been fundamentally altered in him, that the man who climbed down that ladder was not quite the same man who had gone up.

He stopped watching the evening news. When a segment on industrial accidents or chemical plant safety appeared, he would leave the room without explanation. He avoided a former crew member — a man he had known for eleven years — because the man had been present that day, and seeing him brought on a wave of feeling Farid could neither name nor manage. At family gatherings, the presence of his grandchildren and the neighborhood children who came to his son's home had become unexpectedly difficult. The sight of young children playing near adults who could not protect them from something invisible and airborne produced in him a vigilance he could not set aside, even in his own backyard, even when he knew rationally that there was no danger.

At work — Farid still takes occasional small residential jobs, unwilling to fully retire — he finds himself unable to relax on a roof in the way he once could. A colleague's hand on his shoulder to steady him against the wind now produces a sharp, full-body startle that embarrasses him. He lies awake most nights for hours, his body alert in a way his mind cannot override.

What finally brought him to the clinic was his wife's quiet insistence after she found him sitting alone in the kitchen at three in the morning, unable to say what he was afraid of, unable to say he was not. He came, he told the intake clinician, because he did not want his grandchildren to remember him as a man who had disappeared while still alive.
